conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Maya Greene, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported while we take a quick look at how things have been going for you since your baby arrived.

We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us pick up on signs of depression, anxiety, and any thoughts of self-harm that can creep up during the postpartum year. It isn’t a quiz you can “pass” or “fail”; it just gives us a snapshot so we know what kind of care or resources might help you feel more like yourself.

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team who may help with your care—no judgment, no gossip. Feel free to be honest; there are no wrong answers, and many new mothers find it a relief to put feelings into words.

We’ll go through one question at a time, focusing on how you’ve felt over the past seven days. It usually takes about five minutes. Ready to start?

Question 1: Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[small, tired smile]  
Most days I can still laugh—like when my little guy makes those silly milk-bubbles or when my husband tries to swaddle him and ends up tangled in the blanket himself. But I’ve noticed the laughs come out smaller than they used to… almost like I have to remind myself to let it happen. It’s not impossible, just… takes a bit more effort.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes—like when the baby does that little startle in his sleep—it still makes me chuckle, but the laugh feels kind of flat, like I’m going through the motions more than really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do find myself looking forward to little things—like taking the baby for a short walk in the stroller or having my morning coffee—but the excitement isn’t as strong as before. It feels more like “that’ll be nice” instead of “I can’t wait.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week. Yesterday he wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking maybe I’m not reading his cues right, or that I’m doing something wrong as a mom. I know rationally babies just have rough days, but the thought still pops up that I should’ve been able to fix it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A few nights I’ve caught myself lying in bed listening to every little noise from the bassinet, sure something must be wrong even though he’s breathing fine. My heart races and I can’t settle until I’ve checked him two or three times. The worry fades once I see he’s okay, but it keeps sneaking up without any real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—just that fluttery, on-edge feeling when I’m walking to the changing table or when the house gets too quiet. It’s more like a low-level “something’s about to go wrong” hum than an actual scare, and it passes once I distract myself.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like when he cluster-fed and the laundry kept piling up, I felt as if I was drowning in small tasks. I managed to get through them, but it took way more mental energy than it should have, and I ended up crying in the kitchen for a minute after I finally folded the last onesie.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Sleep’s mostly okay—once I get to bed I drift off pretty fast. It’s just that sometimes my mind keeps circling around whether I’m doing enough for him, and that makes it take a little longer to fall asleep, but I wouldn’t say I’m so unhappy that sleep’s impossible.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve had a couple of moments—like yesterday evening when my husband asked how my day was and I just felt this wave of heaviness. Most of the time I’m steady, but yes, I’ve felt that sad, blah feeling a few times this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Just twice this week—once when I couldn’t get him to latch and once when the dishes were overflowing and I felt like I couldn’t keep up. The tears didn’t last long, maybe a minute or two, but yeah, the frustration spilled over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that.

It sounds like you're working very hard to enjoy these first weeks with your baby, yet you've noticed that laughter feels <quote>flat</quote>, excitement is muted, and moments of <sym>tearfulness</sym> and <sym>self-doubt</sym> are creeping in. You described feeling <quote>drowned in small tasks</quote>, lying awake with racing thoughts about whether you're doing <quote>enough for him</quote>, and checking on your little one repeatedly because of nameless worry. At the same time, you are still functioning, getting through each day, and taking pleasure in tiny victories like stroller walks and coffee.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughing only sometimes and describes the laughter as "flat" and mechanical, indicating a clear reduction in ability to enjoy humor, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>"Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, intrusive nighttime worries that compel repeated checking; frequency and intensity fit "sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent low-level anxiety and dread without clear cause, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She describes only occasional overwhelm and eventual completion of tasks, aligning with "sometimes not coping as well as usual"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 14 places you above the threshold (≥14) indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse core symptoms: diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of inadequacy, anxiety, and tearfulness, with functional impact on sleep and coping. While you do not meet full <med>DSM-5</med> criteria on this brief screen, the score warrants urgent follow-up to rule out or confirm clinical depression and to address co-existing <med>generalized anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next week
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, or medication compatible with breastfeeding
3. Use 5-10 min daily relaxation or mindfulness while baby naps; keep room dim and screens off during night feeds to protect sleep
4. Share EPDS results with your partner or support person so they can help watch for worsening mood or anxiety
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after intervention
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Symptom profile (self-report)  
- Reduced enjoyment/pleasure in previously pleasant activities  
- Intermittent tearfulness (2 episodes this week)  
- Low-level persistent worry and hyper-vigilance re infant safety  
- Self-blame / guilt when baby is fussy  
- Episodic feeling “drowned” by routine tasks, with brief crying spell  
- Mild initial-insomnia ruminating about parenting adequacy  
- No anhedonia, no suicidal/harm ideation

Pattern: sub-syndromal depressive and anxiety symptoms emerging in perinatal context; functioning maintained but effort increased.

Screening significance  
- Meets partial criteria for minor/ subsyndromal PPD and perinatal generalized anxiety; does not meet threshold for major depression or panic disorder on brief screen.  
- Protective factors: social support mentioned, no self-harm thoughts.

Recommendation: continue monitoring with EPDS/PHQ-9, consider further perinatal mental health assessment if symptoms worsen or persist >2 weeks.
